This maximum recorded body length, observed in field surveys across the Indo-Pacific, is associated with an asymptotic wet body weight of approximately 2200 grams [Wwi = approximately 2200 grams], derived from length-weight regressions. The species exhibits a robust, laterally compressed body form, with the characteristic rostral horn becoming more pronounced in larger individuals. Comparisons with congeneric species such as Naso vlamingii indicate that the Orangespine unicornfish occupies an intermediate position in terms of maximum size, reflecting its ecological role as a benthic herbivore that forages on macroalgae in reef habitats.

Puberty in Naso lituratus, defined by the onset of gonadal activity, is estimated to occur when individuals reach a total length of approximately 23 cm [Lp = approximately 23 cm]. This length at sexual maturation corresponds to a wet body weight of roughly 278 grams [Wwp = roughly 278 grams], a size at which individuals transition from a predominantly juvenile feeding ecology to one that supports reproductive investment. Field observations indicate that males and females attain this size at a similar age, though subtle differences in growth rates have been noted across geographic regions. The relatively large size at puberty, compared to some other acanthurids, suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes somatic growth before resources are directed toward gamete production.

Spawning events are presumed to occur during lunar periods, with individuals releasing pelagic eggs that are fertilized externally in the water column. The gonadosomatic index can fluctuate seasonally, increasing during peak reproductive months as vitellogenesis proceeds.

The early life stages of Naso lituratus begin with the production of a very small egg; based on an assumed egg diameter of 0.7 millimeters, the calculated wet weight at birth is approximately 0.00018 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00018 grams]. This minute initial mass reflects the pelagic spawning strategy common among acanthurids, where the tiny, buoyant eggs drift with ocean currents. Following fertilization, the yolk-sac larva emerges after a brief incubation period, remaining lecithotrophic until the mouth opens and the onset of exogenous feeding begins. The small size at hatching places the early larva among the most vulnerable stages of the life cycle, subject to high rates of planktonic predation.

Longevity in the Orangespine unicornfish has been estimated at 4745 days [am = 4745 days] when maintained at a water temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], a lifespan that is consistent with the slow growth rates and delayed maturation observed in this species. This maximum lifespan, equivalent to approximately 13 years, places Naso lituratus among the longer-lived members of the Acanthuridae. Age validation studies using otolith micro-increments have supported these estimates, revealing clear annual growth bands that corroborate the longevity data.
